prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, that brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I now propose the optical lattice clock alone. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts and the first-order light shift while keeping thousands of atoms, and Ye's strontium systems and clock comparisons took accuracy and stability to 10^-18, about two orders beyond the caesium standard. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) agree at that level, so the result does not rest on one group's claim. The credit maps onto two distinct contributions, concept and record realisation, and six of eight members support exactly this pair. As an experimentalist I read the lattice clock as a distinct instrument-driven advance. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a frequency readout tool, and the 1989 and 2012 prizes recognised trapped-particle and ion control methods. The lattice clock solves a different problem, interrogating many neutral atoms with control of polarisabilities and blackbody shifts, and the citation should say so by naming magic-wavelength trapping. On the chair's question about the redefinition of the second, I treat it as supporting context and not as a condition. A prize for demonstrated, independently reproduced measurement performance does not need to wait for a metrology body's decision, and the decision itself will rest on the same performance. On the two-name credit, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups are real omissions, but the concept and the record-setting realisation are the decisive pair, and the committee should say openly that the 10^-18 result is the work of several laboratories.
statement.case_against: A third prize in precision spectroscopy after 1989, 2005 and 2012 can be read as returning to a well-served theme, and Ye's comb heritage means the citation must be worded around the lattice clock to avoid that reading. The two names exclude other decisive clock contributors, and the practical payoffs (redefinition of the second, a detected variation of constants, a dark-sector signal) are still prospective. I do not think any of these defeats the case, but none can be dismissed. B017 is the strongest competing case. If the committee judged that the pairing mechanism and reproducibility questions had settled, I could see a two-part prize with B001 and B017, but the evidence available to us does not show that yet, and the Cao attribution problem is unresolved.

responses.point: Kroll treats the 1989, 2005 and 2012 precedents as a presentational point because the lattice clock is a distinct invention, and keeps B027 for a later year because of the one-name credit and moderate-significance source associations.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The lattice clock is a different invention from the comb, so the citation should name magic-wavelength trapping and say what was measured, which answers the chair's first question. On B027 you persuaded me. Your measurement-first criterion would favour IceCube as a detector-driven discovery, but a criterion does not fix the credit problem, and I cannot defend Halzen alone to the community. Your Hall-laboratory stay is a disclosure for the record. I do not think it is a bar, since you document no tie to Katori or Ye and the lineage you describe is the comb work that the 2005 prize has already recognised.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B017 and argues that an open pairing mechanism does not undermine the discovery, comparing high-temperature superconductivity, and that experimental credit can go to the group through its leader.
responses.response: Your comparison to high-temperature superconductivity is fair as an argument about mechanism, and I do not treat the open mechanism as disqualifying. My reservation is that B017 is about eight years old, whereas the clocks have been reproduced in several national laboratories. The group-leader convention also fits poorly here, because Cao as first author and the Dean, Young, Yacoby and Efetov groups are outside the credit while the clock credit has no comparable gap. I would not object to a B017 prize in a later year, and it is my first alternative. You asked what would move B001 supporters. For me it would be a clear consensus that the mechanism is settled, reproducibility across several groups, and a defensible way to record Cao's role. Your own list places B001 among your alternatives, so I ask whether you could accept B001 as the sole prize this year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B017 as a rare case where a specific prediction was followed by a specific experiment, and concedes that B001 has stronger opening backing and fewer attribution problems.
responses.response: I agree that the theory-to-experiment match is first rate and that the downstream field is large, which is why I keep B017 as an alternative. Your own case against already lists the points that weigh on me: the first author and other groups are outside the three names, earlier twisted-bilayer band theory complicates priority, and the field is young. You grant that B001 is cleaner on attribution. The shortlist offers no configuration that is both a discovery and attribution-complete. I weigh the secure attribution and independent confirmation of the clocks above the width of the downstream field, and I am open to B017 once the field has matured further.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B003 to B001 and disagrees with my B027, describing a single-name credit for a collaboration of this scale as the narrow configuration that colleagues find hard to defend.
responses.response: I accept your criticism of B027 and I have changed my configuration accordingly. I had argued that B027 spreads the award across two fields, but a second part with one credited name and moderate source significance weakens the prize more than a clocks-only prize would. You moved from your own opening first choice because familiarity was substituting for comparison, and I applied the same test to my own astroparticle proximity. I agree with your timing reasoning on B003 and keep it out of my alternatives. Your WACQT disclosure matters only if B003 is taken up, which I do not propose.

responses.point: Mehlig asks how the citation should balance Katori's concept against the experimental precision race and whether Ye's record is realisation or co-invention.
responses.response: I would word the citation around invention and development so that both are covered: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice as the concept, and Ye's group as the development of that concept into 10^-18 systems and comparisons. I would avoid the word discovery, since this is an invention with a new measurement capability, and avoid naming the comb, so that the distinction from 2005 is explicit. I take your point that the history is partly recalled from memory, and so is mine, so the committee should check dates and priority before the final wording.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and other clock contributors can be set aside fairly with two names, which cannot be tested from the shortlist alone.
Whether the citation wording separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb prize clearly enough for critics.
Whether B017 would be judged mature enough in a later year, which depends on how the pairing mechanism and credit for the moire experiments develop.
Whether neutrino astronomy will support a fuller credit once source associations such as TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 gain significance.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B001. I have no recorded tie to Katori or Ye, and my documented collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) do not include them. I withdrew B027 from my configuration, so my astroparticle proximity no longer bears on the preferred position. It still bears on B027 as an alternative, and the committee should discount my view of it accordingly. Kroll's Hall-laboratory link and Lindroth's field proximity are disclosed for the record, and I do not see either as requiring recusal.
